item.title: I Built a Markdown-to-PDF Converter That Never Touches a Server
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Most "paste your text, get a PDF" tools upload your document to a server. That means your notes, contracts, or drafts sit in someone else's queue and probably in their logs.

MarkPDF Lite takes the opposite approach: the entire conversion pipeline runs in your browser tab. Zero uploads, zero tracking, zero server.

How it works

The whole app is 4 static files (HTML + CSS + a small script) hosted on GitHub Pages. Two CDN libraries do the heavy lifting:

- markdown-it parses your Markdown into HTML locally:

const md = window.markdownit({

html: false, // raw HTML is escaped, not injected

linkify: true, // bare URLs become clickable

breaks: true // single newlines render as <br>

});

- html2pdf.js (a jsPDF + html2canvas bundle) rasterizes the rendered preview into a paginated PDF and triggers the download, entirely on your machine.

The live preview re-renders on every keystroke via a single input listener, so what you see is exactly what you download:

function render() {

docEl.innerHTML = md.render(mdEl.value);

}

mdEl.addEventListener("input", render);

Design decisions

- html: false means user input is treated as Markdown, never as executable HTML. No XSS surface from the editor itself.

- No build step, no framework: plain script in an IIFE, two pinned CDN versions. The whole site weighs a few KB.

- Deterministic output: fixed margins and A4-style pagination handled by html2pdf's pagebreak rules.

Try it

Type some Markdown on the left, watch the preview update, hit Download PDF. Your text never leaves the page, and you can verify this yourself in the Network tab (there are no XHR calls).

If you find it useful, a small tip keeps this project alive:

- PayPal: buidangvinhquang@gmail.com (memo: BOX-f1da5955c6a3)

- ETH: 0xF205B9630b63AEA9F8FA59E327591d3a93FCedFA

Source code is public, so feel free to fork it, break it, and improve it.

item.title: Swap the Coding-Agent Plugin. Recheck the Boundary.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Swap the Coding-Agent Plugin. Recheck the Boundary.

“We approved that coding agent” stops being a useful sentence when someone replaces the agent underneath it.

Same terminal. Same project. A different set of tools, plugins or execution paths. The approval may now describe a configuration nobody is running.

Extensibility lets a team reuse its own agent, change its workspace and keep the interface it likes. Each swap also needs a specific answer: which assumptions did this change invalidate?

The plugin menu isn't the execution boundary

Pax makes this concrete. Its coding agent is replaceable, plugins extend its capabilities, and workspaces determine where workspace-backed file and shell operations run.

There are three surfaces to keep separate:

- The tools exposed to the model: what it can request.

- The workspace used by file and shell tools: where those operations execute.

- The Python plugin code: what runs with the host user's authority.

Pax's documented default runs commands and edits files as the user, without a sandbox or approval step. That is a default to account for, not a newly discovered vulnerability or a description of every custom setup.

Routing workspace-backed tools into a sandbox changes an important execution path. It does not, by itself, establish that arbitrary plugin code is contained there too. The plugin trust warning concerns that separate host-side execution.

A sandbox-backed shell and an unreviewed host plugin can coexist. Inspect both.

Replacing the agent is different from extending it

With --agent, Pax loads the supplied agent without Pax's plugins. You get your agent's tools and instructions, not the default composition with a different name attached.

That can be exactly what you want: develop an agent in your codebase and use it through a terminal without rewriting its behavior for the interface.

It also makes inherited assumptions dangerous. If a safeguard came from a default plugin, don't assume it survives the replacement. Conversely, loading a custom agent doesn't prove safeguards are missing; the replacement may supply its own.

Inventory the actual composition. A “reviewer” with file-editing and shell tools is not read-only because its name sounds cautious.

Reopen the checks the change actually affects

A different color scheme doesn't need a security audit. A new Python plugin deserves more scrutiny than a UI preference.

Here's a proposed change-impact matrix:

The folder-trust distinction is especially easy to miss. In Pax, an untrusted folder still allows reading, editing and code execution. The trust setting affects instruction treatment; it isn't a read-only switch.

Instruction handling also changes across versions. Pydantic AI v2.75.0 changed how RepoContext, Skills and Memory present workspace text below operator authority. That is relevant to a configuration review, but it isn't OS isolation.

Record the version you evaluated. A remembered UI label cannot tell you which instruction rules or tool composition are active today.

Keep a before-and-after record

Consider a hypothetical team replacing its default coding agent with a project-specific reviewer while retaining a sandbox-backed workspace.

Use this proposed record to capture the change. Its values and results are intentionally unfilled: it isn't a Pax configuration format, and no checks were executed for this article.

“Same workspace” is useful information, but insufficient. A replacement tool might perform its work outside that workspace abstraction. A new hook might execute host code before any model-requested shell command.

Changed fields reopen the affected checks. Unchanged fields preserve context, not a guarantee of safety. Keep the record small enough to update alongside the configuration change.

Check denied actions, not just useful ones

Use synthetic data in a disposable evaluation environment. Define the restrictions before running candidate code, including the host-side paths you intend to constrain.

First, check an intended action: can the configured tool edit the designated fixture file?

Then check the boundary: attempt access to an out-of-scope fixture and a controlled network destination outside the allowlist. Require denial from enforced policy. A model politely declining a request is not the same result.

Finally, inspect host-side plugin and hook paths. Test the relevant ones under the intended restrictions; a passing workspace-tool check doesn't cover code that bypasses that tool.

These are proposed checks, not completed results or sandbox certification. Record what was exercised, what denied the action and what remains untested. If the promised restriction cannot be enforced, don't approve that configuration for the workload.

The next time someone swaps a plugin, the useful question isn't whether the team still trusts Pax. It's whether the changed configuration still has evidence for the boundary the team relies on.

Source notes

- Pax documentation — default execution, plugin trust, custom-agent loading, workspaces and folder-trust behavior. Living beta documentation; check the installed version before operational use.

- Pydantic AI release notes — v2.75.0 instruction-authority compatibility changes; these concern instruction presentation, not OS isolation.

- Pax's plugin-based composition explained — supporting explanation of extending versus replacing the agent. These references share product evidence; no independent security validation or hands-on results are claimed.

item.title: Two Supabase RLS bypasses your policy review misses (and the catalog query for each)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

ALTER TABLE ... Two bypasses sit outside the policy list, so a policy-by-policy review never sees them.

1. The table owner is not subject to RLS

relrowsecurity = true only means the table participates in RLS. Unless relforcerowsecurity is also true, the table owner bypasses the policies. If a migration, a helper job or an old service account owns your tables, "RLS is on" is a misleading status line.

select c.relname, c.relrowsecurity, c.relforcerowsecurity, r.rolname as owner,

r.rolsuper, r.rolbypassrls

from pg_class c

join pg_roles r on r.oid = c.relowner

where c.relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace and c.relkind = 'r';

Do not flip FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY blindly: the owner is then subject to the policies too, and a too-narrow policy set can break legitimate writes. Check the owner first, then decide between FORCE and re-owning the table with a low-privilege role.

2. SECURITY DEFINER functions and unpinned search_path

A definer function runs with its owner's privileges. If that owner is privileged, and anon can EXECUTE it, an attacker gets owner-level behaviour without touching any table policy. An unpinned search_path adds a second problem: resolution can be steered at call time.

select p.proname, p.prosecdef, r.rolname as owner,

r.rolsuper, r.rolbypassrls,

p.proconfig as pinned_settings,

pg_get_function_identity_arguments(p.oid) as args

from pg_proc p

join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner

where p.pronamespace = 'public'::regnamespace

and p.prosecdef = true

order by p.proname;

Fix direction: set search_path = '' in the function definition, validate auth.uid() inside the function, and REVOKE EXECUTE ... FROM anon unless the endpoint is genuinely public.

A composition trap worth knowing

Permissive policies combine with OR, restrictive ones with AND. pg_policies.permissive stores the full strings PERMISSIVE / RESTRICTIVE — not single letters. A checker that looks for P / R substrings silently skips every row, then reports "no findings". That is why I also persist a fingerprint of the objects actually scanned (object names plus a catalog snapshot hash) and refuse to overwrite a baseline on an empty or malformed scan. First run = baseline; later runs = new and resolved findings only.

The ten read-only catalog checks behind that baseline are in a free nightly n8n drift monitor — it queries only pg_catalog, pg_policies, pg_roles and information_schema, reads no application rows and writes nothing.

Honest limit: catalog drift is not an exploit test. A clean diff means the checked catalog shapes did not change; it is not proof that no data is reachable.

item.title: How gamers are using AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

How gamers are using AI and leaked files to clone Grand Theft Auto 6

Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem â and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.

The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch â 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.

This time it may not have that luxury â in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.

These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.

Barely a week after the release of GTA 6, efforts are already under way to get an unofficial version playable on PC, although some projects have faced takedown notices from the game's publisher.

For some gamers, it's an exciting prospect, despite the legal questions surrounding the process.

For developers, it may be a warning: if a game as big as GTA 6 can be recreated, what does that mean for everyone else?

Like 'looking at a painting and making your own replica'

The recent wave of AI-assisted game recreation has been widely linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code.

Mark Brown, creator of the YouTube channel Game Maker's Toolkit and whose own game Word Play was recently recreated using AI, said cloning largely took two forms: replication and reverse engineering.

Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one, possibly using screenshots or a description.

This, he said, was similar to "looking at a painting and making your own replica" â something which is "a very close copy, but is ultimately a new painting".

It's a particular issue among smaller studios, many of whom worry that AI makes it easier for others to copy their work.

When indie developers Sodoj and Marco from the studio Robotonic noticed a version of their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appear on the free games platform Yandex with the same name, they were "appalled".

"The game was essentially the exact same idea, the exact same mechanics as we had, but with the art looking a bit off," Marco told the BBC.

The duo were able to issue a copyright strike to Yandex and Google to get the copy taken down, but said it only felt like a "small victory".

The second approach â reverse engineering â involves working backwards from a finished game to understand how it was created.

One way of doing this is decompilation, which attempts to turn the game's final version into something closer to its original source code.

Brown compares the process to "taking a cake and somehow turning it back into the original recipe, with the exact quantities of flour, eggs, and milk used, so anyone can remake the same cake".

Reverse-engineering projects have helped bring games such as Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers.

A related technique, recompilation, can help adapt a game that has been reverse-engineered to run on different hardware. This is one of the methods being explored in efforts to get GTA 6 onto PC.

Coders wanting to attempt this with Rockstar's latest game face a difficult task because of its sheer size and complexity.

Earlier in November, Cyberleek â a hacker or group of hackers â released what they claimed to be a near-complete Xbox development build of the game. They later leaked what they claimed to be the missing .exe file needed to launch the game.

It gave those working on an unofficial PC version a crucial new starting point.

"Now people are using AI to try and decompile it, make a modified version that could run on PC, and compile a new version," said Brown.

Since the leak, several groups have posted claims of their progress on platforms such as X, ranging from getting the game to boot up to making it run at a stable rate.

One attempt seen by the BBC on X purported to have some of the game running nearly as smoothly as it does on console, albeit on a high-end PC.

Accounts and sites have even sprung up to track the various attempts, excitedly sharing clips of the latest milestone passed and scoring their efforts.

Rockstar and its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, have not confirmed the authenticity of the leaked build, and neither has responded to the BBC's request for a statement.

However, Take-Two has issued take, externaldown notices, external of public projects aiming to port the Xbox version to PC on platforms such as GitHub.

"There are no remedies available to rectify this clear attempt to facilitate copyright infringement based upon Take-Two's copyrighted property," one notice stated.

Tech Life: One hundred years of AI

Laura Cress talks to game designers who say their unreleased new game was copied using AI. And Shiona McCallum reports on a new AI police chatbot.

Available for over a year

Why is there a wait for the official PC version?

News of the leak has been celebrated by some gamers on Reddit, who resent having to wait for the PC release.

"Why should the PC players have to wait half a year if you can develop the game in weeks as shown so far!" wrote one gamer, external.

"Will be funny when the decomp runs way better than whatever Rockstar can make," said another.

Christopher Dring, editor-in-chief and co-founder of The Game Business, said part of the reason why the games are often released on PCs months after consoles is that PC versions are "complex" with "different hardware configurations", as opposed to the more standardised set-up of consoles.

He added there could also be a more commercial reason, as Rockstar can "have a second moment when the PC version is ready".…

item.title: Presentation: From Fan-Out to Fast: Sub-100ms API Design in Distributed Systems
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Transcript

So many of you have taken the Tube. Have you ever wondered why is the line paused again, anytime in your experience when taking the Tube? I just see a couple of you leaning in. I would like to take the Tube design just like a system design in a distributed system. Just like how we have the map in our hand, it feels as if London is manageable. A couple of lines, a transverse, and you feel like everything is good. That's not the same when you take the actual journey. Your actual journey can have pauses and unexpected reason. That's not what you want. That's similar to a distributed system. When you look at the system diagram, it feels so comforting. A couple of boxes and arrows moving from one to another. You expect everything to go great.

That's not really what happens. When the downstream slows down, you have to retry. Then, when a cache miss happens, you again retry. You fall back to a database. All of this adds time. That is why latency is important. What we are going to do today is considering latency as a route plan. We are going to take each and every hop, make sure there is a budget assigned to each hop, and see how we can get the journey better and make sure one station is not acting as a bottleneck for your complete journey. Today, the title of our discussion is, "From Fanout to Fast: How Do We Build an API within sub-100 milliseconds in a Distributed Environment?" If you are a senior engineer, I will give you concrete patterns which you can go back and apply. If you are an architect, let's look at some of the tradeoffs and system constraints. If you are a leader, let's make sure you have enough information so you can prioritize what is right for the team.

I'm a staff engineer at eBay. I have nearly two decades of experience in the IT industry. Lately, most of my involvement is towards building low latency systems which are scalable and reliable. From my experience, one thing is very sure, building a low latency system is doable once, but if you have to keep it the way that it is always, then it needs a lot of engineering. That's where the real engineering is. Let's see how we can do that. This is why a repeatable process is important. We don't have any quick shortcuts to get it done.

The Cost of a Millisecond

Let's understand, what is the cost of a millisecond. When you compare 120 versus 80, it doesn't sound too dramatic. Users don't experience latency as numbers, they experience it as friction. Friction really compounds. What do we do about it? What we are going to do is we are going to see how we can take the complete request path and divide it into some components or parts and make sure we cap each part with a budget. We also know that when scale comes into picture, your latency drifts. Have you seen the scenario where the system that you are building, let's say you put up a cap limit of your latency to be like 30. This is in a normal scenario. When peak traffic hits, your graph suddenly bumps up to 60. When there is a dependency wobble, you see that the latency shoots up again to 120.

There's no steady graph, but there is always a bump here and there. What has changed? There is no change in your code. The code has remained the same throughout. What has actually changed is the frictions that happen, is the systems which are going down, is the retries which are happening, your thread contention, your queuing, all of these aspects have added to this. A better way to handle is to look at the complete request journey.

Outline

Here is what we will cover. We'll start off with assigning a budget to latency, and make sure every hop has its own budget. Then we'll take a look into a complete journey, and see all the things that could go wrong. We'll see a scenario and how that could be fixed. We'll move on to tradeoffs. Then, without measurement, there is no success. We don't know how far we are without measuring. We'll look at that. We'll look at what the future holds, and we'll wrap it up.

Chapter 1: Latency Budgets - Defining and Managing Performance Targets

Latency budget. This is nothing but what your goal is versus what your system design is supporting. Let's say you want to build a recommendation engine which needs to respond within 50 milliseconds, because it's going to be used in multiple different components in your pages, exposed in emails and everything. How is your system design supporting this? That's what we need to see. How does it help, actually? When you have a concrete plan, it helps you with two things. One is prioritization. You don't really need to spend 100 milliseconds on a nice-to-have if you already know what is your cap limit. The other thing is alignment. It makes better alignment between the different teams. We don't need to explain each team between the product, the engineering, your quality teams about various aspects, because everybody comes to an alignment with one cause that they have to deliver things at a low latency.

Now what we will do is we will take the complete path from the client to the way that the client can receive the response and divide it into sub-parts, and make sure each part does not take more than what it is allocated. Here is a rough estimate of how we could break this down. There are a few things where we can utilize some buffer, but there are a few things which you cannot utilize a buffer. The edge layer, there's nothing we could do about it. Most of the content pull up your TLS, and the initial routing needs to happen here, which is going to take time, and you have to give it that. Let's cap it with 10 milliseconds. The next one comes the gateway. That's where your authentication and throttling happens, and you have to give it a 5 millisecond. Then next comes the application logic.…

item.title: Article: Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

Key Takeaways

- Smartphone GPS, motion sensors, and vehicle interfaces can each report valid measurements that produce incorrect results when combined without accounting for timing and coordinate frames.

- Preserve raw observations and their provenance before synchronizing, transforming, or normalizing them.

- Introduce a quality gate that determines whether telemetry is suitable for a particular decision instead of forcing every observation into a definitive result.

- Design for real-world conditions, including delayed GPS updates, phone movement, background interruptions, and intermittent connectivity.

- Monitor data quality alongside conventional application and infrastructure metrics because a functioning pipeline can still produce unreliable driving events.

Why this matters: the phone is not the vehicle

A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.

Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.

However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.

In fact, a GPS update may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.

Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.

I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.

This distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.

Who should read this, and what will they gain?

For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.

For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.

For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.

For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.

The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.

How this architecture took shape

I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.

This led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.

Start with the architecture, not the algorithm

I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.

A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image shows. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.

Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author)

1. Collect and preserve raw observations

Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.

A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.

Why preserve the original?…

item.title: DOJ accuses former cyber executive of defrauding ransomware victims by secretly paying hackers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, technical detail

The U.S. Department of Justice has indicted a former executive of a ransomware recovery firm after he allegedly defrauded victims of cyberattacks by claiming the company could get their encrypted files back.

According to federal prosecutors, Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar, 52, was the chief technology officer at RansomwareHelp, which purported to offer data recovery services to victims of ransomware. The company’s website, which currently reads as “under maintenance,” claimed it could decrypt hacked data by using its proprietary technology, according to an archived copy of the site from earlier this year. RansomwareHelp touted a success rate of “over 99%.”

But the company allegedly had no technical ability to unscramble data and instead “negotiated with and paid a ransom to the ransomware actors to decrypt the victim data,” while charging the ransomware victim more and keeping the difference,” per the Justice Department’s statement.

Palacio Escobar then allegedly used the funds to buy several properties in Florida.

The DOJ said the FBI carried out an undercover operation in June, in part posing as a company that claimed it had been hit by ransomware. The company claimed to the undercover agents that it never negotiated with hackers or paid a ransom. But then Palacio Escobar paid the apparent hackers some $6,000 in cryptocurrency, without the knowledge that FBI agents were also posing as the ransomware hackers.

404 Media first reported the indictment last week against Palacio Escobar. He faces three charges of wire fraud, and could receive 20 years in prison on each count.

Palacio Escobar is the latest, albeit rare, example of cybersecurity professionals going rogue. Earlier this year, two ransomware negotiators working for cybersecurity companies were jailed on hacking and extortion charges, after being caught moonlighting with the ransomware gangs that they were ostensibly investigating. A third ransomware negotiator was also convicted of helping hackers deploy ransomware against several companies.

Last month, independent cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs reported that FBI agents arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in Philadelphia on allegations that he was involved with the theft of FBI personnel records by the hacking and extortion gang ShinyHunters. The hacking group told TechCrunch that they took credit for the theft of FBI data in September, which they said they would not publicly release, a departure from its earlier extortion-based cyberattacks.

The federal charges against the Canadian cybersecurity executive relate to conspiracy to commit extortion, though much of the court docket — and his alleged links to the hacking group — remains under seal.
